title: next/image: On-Demand Sharp Resizing & WebP/AVIF Conversion

progressiveExplaining.eli5: If you take a photo with a giant camera, you don't send the huge 10MB poster to a tiny smartphone. An assistant standing in the middle takes your original photo, shrinks it to the exact phone screen size, converts it to a super-compressed modern format (like WebP or AVIF), and hands it over in a flash. `next/image` is that smart assistant.
progressiveExplaining.junior: `next/image` extends HTML `` with automatic image optimization. It serves images in modern formats (AVIF/WebP), automatically generates responsive `srcset` attributes based on device sizes, resizes images on-demand on the server using the high-performance `sharp` library, and prevents Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) by requiring explicit `width`/`height` or `fill`.
progressiveExplaining.senior: Architecturally, `next/image` is an image transformation proxy. When the client browser requests a page, Next.js generates an `` tag pointing to `/_next/image?url=...&w=...&q=...`. The optimizer parses the `Accept` header to negotiate AVIF/WebP format delivery, resizes the asset using libvips/sharp in a worker pool, caches the optimized binary on the edge/file system, and returns proper immutable caching headers.
progressiveExplaining.underTheHood: The image optimization pipeline runs through the internal Next.js image endpoint. It hashes the target URL, width, and quality parameters into a cache key. If a cache miss occurs, the image optimizer fetches upstream bytes (local or allowed remote patterns), validates SVG/malicious headers, passes buffers into `sharp` via C++ bindings for resizing/transcoding, writes the output to `.next/cache/images`, and responds with `Content-Type: image/avif` or `image/webp`.

interviewGotchas.question: Why does `next/image` require external domains to be configured in `next.config.js`?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: Interviewers test your awareness of server-side security and Denial of Service (DoS) protection.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: Because `next/image` proxies and transforms images on the server on demand, an open optimizer without domain whitelisting would act as an open proxy. Attackers could flood `/_next/image?url=https://attacker.com/huge.png` to consume CPU, memory, and bandwidth. Next.js enforces `images.remotePatterns` to strictly whitelist authorized upstream asset origins.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: Never use wide-open wildcard patterns (`hostname: '**'`) in production configs as it exposes the optimization server to SSRF and DoS vectors.

interviewGotchas.question: When should you use the `fill` prop instead of `width` and `height`?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: This checks practical responsive CSS layout integration.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: Use `fill` when the exact pixel dimensions are unknown in advance (e.g. dynamic responsive cards or background hero sections). With `fill`, the image styles automatically set `position: absolute; inset: 0; width: 100%; height: 100%;`. The parent element must explicitly specify `position: relative`, `position: fixed`, or `position: absolute` with a designated aspect ratio or height.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: Using `fill` on an element whose parent is statically positioned will cause the image to expand across the nearest positioned ancestor or the entire viewport.
